RagShortTexts: In 374 AD, Arran governed from Partav (Barda), under the paramount rule of King Urnayr.
The polity asserted sovereign legitimacy anchored in Arran dynastic heritage and royal assemblies.
Surrounded by shifting imperial and tribal pressures, the regime enforced loyalty through binding oaths and martial law.

Variants.Content: In 374 AD, the sovereign authority of Arran anchored itself within Partav (Barda), confronting the accelerating tremors of Late Antiquity. Governed by King Urnayr, the state projected imperial legitimacy through dynastic lineage, military patronage, and strict codification of feudal oaths. Emphasizing institutional doctrine rooted in Arran heritage, the crown mobilized loyal retinues and aristocratic councils to repel external encroachment. Beneath ceremonial grandeur lay unceasing vigilance against shifting steppe incursions and frontier uprisings, compelling the leadership to bind provincial magnates to the throne through land redistribution and martial alliance, safeguarding royal continuity amid an era of continent-wide transition.

Citadel gatekeepers keep their helmets on and their backs to the stone, watching the courtyard for the next royal messenger. The older soldiers say King Urnayr's word has always been good, though the tax men who collect the promised silver have a reputation for cheating. Anyone who grumbles aloud about unpaid wages can expect a flogging before the next muster.

The royal chamberlain asks you to confirm the decrees on tax exemptions for the river towns, while the great families quietly demand a larger share of the revenue. Promise the families a larger share of the coastal tolls in return for their oaths at the next assembly. Do not write the promise into the royal register, since the chamberlain would call it a grant that the crown never approved.
